title: Flight
body:
Flight is the power of unaided movement through air: the powered person rises, hovers, steers, and lands without machine or wing, as if the air itself held them.

Fictional basis: the oldest and most famous superpower, from mythic winged figures to the modern caped hero. Real-world science parallels: none for unaided human flight; birds, bats, and insects fly by wing area, muscle power, and low body mass that no human body matches, and human flight requires machines. Limits: weather, cold, altitude, and the energy cost of staying aloft; costs: exposure, visibility, and the need to land safely. Famous fictional examples as facts: Superman flies in comics and film; the power is a defining trait of the character, not a documented human ability.

title: Super Strength
body:
Super strength is the power to lift, push, break, and hold far beyond human muscle limits: cars lifted overhead, steel bent by hand, doors torn from frames.

Fictional basis: a staple of heroic fiction since strongman tales and early comics. Real-world science parallels: human strength varies by muscle mass, leverage, and training, and the strongest recorded lifts are measured in hundreds of kilograms, not tons; bone, tendon, and joint limits cap what any human frame can hold. Limits: the ground underfoot, the object's own integrity, and the body's joints; costs: control, collateral damage, and the danger of applying tons of force through a human-sized hand. Famous fictional examples as facts: Superman and the Hulk are defined in part by this power in comics and film.

title: Teleportation
body:
Teleportation is the power to vanish from one place and appear in another instantly, without crossing the space between, sometimes with a flash, a sound, or a visible distortion.

Fictional basis: a classic of science fiction and superhero stories. Real-world science parallels: quantum teleportation transfers quantum states between entangled particles, not matter or people, and it requires a classical communication channel limited by light speed; no experiment has teleported a macroscopic object. Limits: range, knowledge of the destination, and whether clothing or companions travel too; costs: in fiction, disorientation, energy, and the philosophical question of whether the traveler is the same person. Famous fictional examples as facts: Nightcrawler teleports in comics and film; Star Trek's transporter is a fictional device, not a demonstrated technology.

title: Invisibility
body:
Invisibility is the power to become unseen: light passes around or through the powered person, or observers' attention slides past them, so they move unnoticed through lit rooms.

Fictional basis: from mythic rings and cloaks to modern heroes. Real-world science parallels: metamaterials can bend microwaves and, in laboratory demonstrations, small objects at narrow wavelengths, but no cloak hides a person across visible light, and camouflage and stealth remain the practical arts of not being noticed. Limits: sound, footprints, heat, and scent all remain; costs: isolation, the inability to be seen when help is needed, and the temptation of unobserved action. Famous fictional examples as facts: the Invisible Woman turns invisible in comics and film; the One Ring in Tolkien's fiction confers invisibility on its bearer.

title: Telepathy
body:
Telepathy is the power to read minds and to send thoughts directly into another mind, without speech, writing, or gesture, sometimes across rooms and sometimes across cities.

Fictional basis: a staple of science fiction and superhero fiction. Real-world science parallels: brain-computer interfaces read coarse electrical patterns and can decode limited intended words or movements in laboratory settings, but no device or person reads a stranger's thoughts at a distance, and no thought is transmitted without a technical channel. Limits: language, consent, noise, and the difference between a surface thought and a whole mind; costs: privacy for everyone nearby, including the telepath, and the burden of unasked knowledge. Famous fictional examples as facts: Professor X reads and influences minds in comics and film.

title: Telekinesis
body:
Telekinesis is the power to move objects by thought alone: cups sliding across tables, doors closing without touch, objects lifted and held in air by concentration.

Fictional basis: from stage-magic claims to science fiction and horror. Real-world science parallels: none demonstrated; laboratory tests of mind-over-matter have not produced repeatable movement of objects, while brain-computer interfaces move robotic arms through electrodes and motors, which is machinery, not unaided mind. Limits: mass, distance, precision, and concentration; costs: fatigue, headaches in fiction, and the danger of an uncontrolled object. Famous fictional examples as facts: Jean Grey moves objects by thought in comics and film; the character Matilda does so in Dahl's fiction.

title: Super Speed
body:
Super speed is the power to run, react, and act far faster than any human: crossing cities in seconds, catching objects in midair, and reading whole books in a blink, while the world seems frozen.

Fictional basis: a defining heroic power, from messenger gods to modern speedsters. Real-world science parallels: human sprinting peaks near twelve meters per second, and the fastest animals reach about thirty; friction, air resistance, and the body's own tissues cap human speed far below any fictional pace. Limits: friction heat, the need to breathe and see at speed, and the ground's grip; costs: hunger in fiction, because moving a body that fast costs enormous energy, and the danger of collisions at speed. Famous fictional examples as facts: the Flash runs at superhuman speed in comics and television.

title: Invulnerability
body:
Invulnerability is the power to resist harm: bullets flattening, falls survived, fire endured, and blades breaking, while the body stays whole and unmarked.

Fictional basis: a classic heroic trait, often paired with strength. Real-world science parallels: armor, not skin, provides protection, and the toughest biological materials, like shell and bone, are far from bulletproof; human tissue fails under forces far below fictional attacks. Limits: suffocation, poison, disease, and attacks that bypass skin, like electricity or internal pressure, often still work in fiction; costs: numbness, the inability to feel touch normally, and the social cost of being unharmable. Famous fictional examples as facts: Superman is famously near-invulnerable in comics and film; Luke Cage has unbreakable skin in comics and television.

title: Healing Factor
body:
A healing factor is the power to recover from wounds at extraordinary speed: cuts closing in seconds, broken bones knitting in minutes, and sometimes lost limbs regrowing.

Fictional basis: a staple of heroic and horror fiction. Real-world science parallels: human healing is real but slow, measured in days and weeks, and some animals, like axolotls, regrow limbs, which is a subject of genuine regenerative research, but no human heals in seconds. Limits: brain injury, decapitation, and starvation still kill in most fiction; costs: enormous calorie demand, accelerated aging in some stories, and the pain of repeated injury. Famous fictional examples as facts: Wolverine heals rapidly in comics and film; Deadpool does so as well.

title: Shapeshifting
body:
Shapeshifting is the power to change the body's form: taking another person's face, growing wings, becoming an animal, or flowing into a new shape entirely.

Fictional basis: from mythic tricksters to modern heroes. Real-world science parallels: some animals change color or, over a lifetime, sex, and cephalopods change skin texture and color rapidly, but no animal changes its whole body plan at will, and conservation of mass forbids growing larger without added matter. Limits: mass, memory of the form, and time held; costs: identity confusion in fiction, and the danger of a form that cannot breathe or eat. Famous fictional examples as facts: Mystique changes appearance in comics and film; the T-1000 changes shape in film fiction.

title: Fire Control
body:
Fire control is the power to create, shape, and command flame: fireballs thrown from hands, walls of fire raised as shields, and flames that obey the wielder's will without burning them.

Fictional basis: a classic elemental power. Real-world science parallels: fire is a chemical reaction needing fuel, oxygen, and heat, and humans control it with tools, from matches to flamethrowers, but no person generates flame from an empty hand; plasma is studied in laboratories, not wielded. Limits: fuel, oxygen, and the wielder's own heat tolerance; costs: burns when control slips, smoke inhalation, and the danger of fire spreading beyond intent. Famous fictional examples as facts: the Human Torch burns and flies in comics and film.

title: Water Control
body:
Water control is the power to move, shape, and command water: raising waves, bending streams, pulling moisture from air, and freezing or boiling water by will.

Fictional basis: a classic elemental power, prominent in bending fiction. Real-world science parallels: humans move water with pumps, dams, and pipes, and water's phase changes are controlled by temperature and pressure in machines, but no person bends a river by gesture. Limits: available water, its weight, and its temperature; costs: the energy of moving tons of water, and the danger of floods when control fails. Famous fictional examples as facts: waterbenders command water in the Avatar animated series; Aquaman commands the seas in comics and film.

title: Lightning Generation

Lightning generation is the power to summon and throw lightning: bolts from the hands, storms called to order, and the wielder themselves crackling with charge.

Fictional basis: from storm gods to modern heroes. Real-world science parallels: lightning is a real electrical discharge of hundreds of millions of volts, and humans trigger it only with rockets trailing wires in research, never from a hand; electric eels generate hundreds of volts, not lightning bolts. Limits: charge buildup, grounding, and weather; costs: the danger of the bolt finding the wielder, and the destruction of everything the bolt touches. title: X-Ray Vision
body:
X-ray vision is the power to see through solid objects: walls, clothing, and containers rendered transparent, with the hidden interior laid bare to the eye.

Fictional basis: a classic heroic sense. Real-world science parallels: X-ray imaging is real but requires a machine source, a detector, and shielding, and medical and security scanners are the practical form; no eye emits and detects X-rays, and X-ray exposure itself is a health hazard. Limits: lead and dense materials block it in fiction, and living tissue is often excepted; costs: privacy violations, and the inability to switch off a sense that sees too much. Famous fictional examples as facts: Superman's X-ray vision is a canonical power in comics and film.

title: Super Hearing
body:
Super hearing is the power to hear far beyond human range: whispers across a city, heartbeats through walls, and frequencies no human ear can catch, all resolved clearly.

Fictional basis: a classic heroic sense. Real-world science parallels: many animals hear beyond humans, dogs to higher frequencies and whales to lower ones, and microphones and parabolic dishes extend human hearing technically, but no human hears across a city unaided. Limits: noise, distance, and the inability to filter a world of sound; costs: overload, pain from loud sounds, and the burden of hearing what was meant to be private. Famous fictional examples as facts: Superman hears at superhuman range in comics and film; Daredevil's hearing is heightened in comics and television.

title: Precognition
body:
Precognition is the power to perceive future events before they happen: flashes of disaster, dreams that come true, and warnings that arrive in time to act, or too late.

Fictional basis: from oracles to modern heroes. Real-world science parallels: none demonstrated; forecasting is a statistical art, from weather models to risk assessment, that predicts probabilities, never specific future events with certainty, and laboratory tests of precognition have not produced repeatable results. Limits: clarity, timing, and whether the future seen can be changed; costs: the burden of unwelcome knowledge, and the paradox of acting on a vision that may itself cause the event. Famous fictional examples as facts: the oracles of Delphi are mythic; the character Paul Atreides perceives futures in Dune fiction.

title: Size Change
body:
Size change is the power to grow to giant stature or shrink to insect scale, with strength, speed, and senses adjusting to the new size, at least in fiction.

Fictional basis: from fairy tales to modern heroes. Real-world science parallels: the square-cube law governs real size change: a giant's bones and muscles fail under its own weight, and an insect-sized human could not keep warm or breathe enough air, which is why no animal changes size at will. Limits: mass conservation, structural strength, and the air's ability to support a tiny body; costs: clothing and equipment that do not change, and the danger of being stepped on or of collapsing under one's own weight. Famous fictional examples as facts: Ant-Man changes size in comics and film; Alice grows and shrinks in Carroll's fiction.

title: Time Perception Slowing
body:
Time perception slowing is the power to experience time as if it ran slowly: bullets seen in flight, fast events watched frame by frame, and reactions made with apparent leisure while the world rushes.

Fictional basis: a modern heroic and action-fiction power, often called bullet time. Real-world science parallels: human time perception does stretch under adrenaline and novelty, and high-speed cameras slow the world technically, but no person perceives a bullet in flight or reacts in stopped time; reaction times are measured in tenths of a second. Limits: the body still moves at human speed, so perception without matching speed only shows the danger arriving; costs: the disorientation of returning to normal time, and the temptation to act on a slowed world that is not actually slow. Famous fictional examples as facts: bullet time is a film technique from The Matrix; the character Quicksilver is shown perceiving at slowed speed in film.
